Fallow
fal'o
a. (of ground left unsown and hardened; the prophets' standing figure for a heart that must be broken up before seed is sown — and, once, a colour, in the fallow deer)
From Old English fealg, ploughed land, in the agricultural sense; the colour sense of fallow deer is a different Old English word, fealu, pale yellow. The Hebrew at Jeremiah 4:3 is nir, tillable ground, with the verb nur, to break up.

Biblical Definition

Twice the prophets give the same command in almost the same words, and it is one of the most practical instructions in Scripture concerning repentance. Jeremiah: “For thus saith the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem, Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” (Jeremiah 4:3). Hosea: “Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and rain righteousness upon you” (Hosea 10:12). Fallow ground is not barren ground; it is good ground that has lain unworked until it has crusted over, and the seed cast on it lies on the surface and is taken by birds. The command is therefore not to plant harder but to plough — to break the crust before sowing. Both prophets attach the promise to it: Hosea says the LORD will come and rain righteousness. This is the mind of the parable of the sower long before the parable was spoken, and it is why the Puritans made preparation of heart a labour and not a mood. The Authorized Version's other use is unrelated and simply a species of deer among the clean beasts (Deuteronomy 14:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines fallow as land ploughed and left unsown, or left untilled after a crop — and separately as a pale red or yellow colour, as in the fallow deer.

expand to see more

FALLOW, a. Pale red or pale yellow; as a fallow deer.

2. Unsowed; not tilled; left to rest after a year or more of tillage.

3. Left unsowed after plowing.

FALLOW, n. Land that has lain a year or more untilled or unseeded.

FALLOW, v.i. To fade; to become yellow. To plow, harrow and break land without seeding it.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 4:3 — "For thus saith the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem, Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns."

Hosea 10:12 — "Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and rain righteousness upon you."

Deuteronomy 14:5 — "The hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer, and the wild goat, and the pygarg, and the wild ox, and the chamois."

Matthew 13:7 — "And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them:"

Modern Corruption

Modern evangelism sows harder on unploughed ground, treating decision as the whole work and preparation of heart as legalism.

expand to see more

The dominant method of the last two centuries has been to increase the sowing — more appeals, more meetings, more urgency — on ground nobody has ploughed. Jeremiah forbids exactly this: break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns. Two commands, and the second is a prohibition. Seed scattered on crusted ground and among thorns produces the harvest our Lord described, and the modern anxiety about people who profess and fall away is largely an anxiety about a harvest that was predictable from the method. The older evangelicals understood the difference between conviction and decision, and were prepared to labour a long time in the first before pressing the second.

The corrective must avoid an opposite error, which the Puritan tradition itself sometimes fell into: making preparation a work that qualifies a man for grace, so that sinners wait to be sufficiently broken before they may come to Christ. That is not Hosea's doctrine either. The ploughing is commanded, but the rain is promised and not produced — till he come and rain righteousness upon you. A man does not break up his ground in order to earn the rain; he breaks it up because rain is coming and crusted ground sheds it. The invitation is always immediate; the labour of self-examination is what keeps it from falling on a surface.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nir, tilled or tillable ground — Jeremiah 4:3, Hosea 10:12; nur, to break up ground; yachmur, the fallow deer — Deuteronomy 14:5.

expand to see more

Hebrew nir — freshly tilled ground, a fallow field; Jeremiah 4:3 and Hosea 10:12.

Hebrew nur — to break up untilled ground; the verb of the command in both prophets.

Hebrew qots — thorns; the ground Jeremiah forbids sowing among.

Hebrew yachmur — the fallow deer or roebuck; Deuteronomy 14:5, an unrelated sense.

Old English fealg, ploughed land, and fealu, pale yellow — two different words joined in one English spelling.

Usage

"“Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — a command and a prohibition."

"“Till he come and rain righteousness upon you” — the ploughing is ours, the rain His."

"Fallow ground is good ground crusted over, not barren ground."
